name: PT ESSA Industries Indonesia Tbk.

frontmatter.title: ESSA Industries: ammonia at the bottom of the global cost curve, priced for a collapse
frontmatter.summary: ESSA runs one ammonia train in Central Sulawesi, sells all output to an affiliated trader at a published index and carries net cash. September changes the balance-sheet inputs, not the thesis: BUY on a target of Rp682 is a coverage view, not an actionable trade at the tape, where the registry-prior payoff is below the hurdle. The shares price a collapse the contracted cost base does not justify; the dividend and cash set the floor.
thesis: One train, one offtaker, one gas field: the Luwuk ammonia plant sells its entire output to Genesis at Fertecon index and buys Senoro feedstock under the gas sales agreement signed in October 2026, a cost position most European capacity no longer has [S2, S8, S9].
The market is short a crash it may not get: at Rp488 the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of -17.6%, deeper than our -10.0% base case [S0].

2026 is already earned: nine-month revenue US$310.9m and attributable profit US$51.1m after a major turnaround, with the third quarter the strongest by revenue and profit and realised ammonia at US$531/t in the first half [S3, S4, S0].

The balance sheet is the floor: at the FY2025 year-end the company held US$125.8m of cash against US$0.2m of debt and it still carried net cash at 30 September after paying the Rp52.0/share dividend, capex is guided at US$10.0m to US$20.0m [S0, S7, S6].
We hold gross margin between the FY2023 margin trough and the FY2022 spike and still find value, because the DCF is run on the mid-cycle rather than on the 2026 spike [S2].

The payoff is the discipline, not the rating: on the registry prior and the kill's falsification exit the expected return is below the hurdle, so this is a coverage view and not an actionable trade at the tape [S2, S8].

blocks.text: What changed in this results update, and what did not. The nine-month figures we carried in the initiation are now confirmed in the pack, which also brings the 30 September balance sheet; the third quarter was the strongest of the year and lifted nine-month revenue to US$310.9m and attributable profit to US$51.1m. The one number we do not use raw is the pack's nine-month cost of revenue: the quarterly cost line exists only in the data pack, no archived filing carries it, and the same pack reports quarterly D&A an order of magnitude below the LK, so we hold the FY2026E gross margin at the nine-month run-rate less about half a point — 37.7% in the model, against the low thirty-eights the pack's nine-month cost line implies — rather than at that nine-month figure itself [S0, S4]. We have re-marked the PAU minority from book to its economic share, including its share of net cash, and the quarter's balance sheet works the other way, lifting the book minority the engine deducts and showing working capital rebuilt after the June swing. The net effect is a twelve-month target of Rp682. The call is unchanged in direction and weaker in degree.

We stay at BUY on PT ESSA Industries Indonesia with a twelve-month target of Rp682, 39.7% above the Rp488 price and 53.9% total return once the Rp70 of dividends we expect over the next twelve months is added. The target is the probability-weighted average of three scenario values — Rp365 on a faster ammonia normalisation, Rp743 on our most likely path and Rp876 if European curtailment persists — rolled forward a year at the cost of equity and net of the interim dividend.

Two probabilities must not be confused, and the previous version did. The scenario weights are the chance of each value path, not the probability that the shares beat the price: the weighted target sitting above the tape is the arithmetic of a large up-leg, not evidence that upside is the likely outcome. We carry the probability of upside at the registry base rate for a commodity capex turnaround — forty-two in a hundred, the same prior the desk committed on 11 November when it judged the trade killed — and we do not move that prior without a new registry commit.

The reconciliation of that kill needs the arithmetic, not an assertion. The kill's target was six hundred and eighty-seven rupiah, five rupiah from the Rp682 published here, so the previous version was wrong to describe it as a further haircut to the same model lines. The ruling was a payoff finding, not an entry-price objection: on the kill's own convention — exit at the falsification price of three hundred rupiah, not at a fair value, with the Rp70 dividend received in both states — the up leg is 39.7% plus the dividend and the down leg is roughly minus a quarter. At the forty-two per cent prior that is an expected twelve-month return of roughly nine per cent, below the ten point four four per cent a year hurdle and below the eight point four to nine point three per cent ceiling the desk found on 11 November at a lower tape. The earlier draft's claim that the expected return cleared the hurdle came only from substituting the Rp365 bear fair value for the falsification exit; that substitution lifts the arithmetic to the mid-teens but understates the downside the bear weight exists to carry. A higher tape and a target five rupiah below the kill's leave the payoff worse, not better, and no new sourced evidence since 11 November moves the ceiling. So the rating is the house's target-based classification — the 53.9% total return to Rp682 — and it is a coverage view, not an actionable trade at Rp488: on the registry prior the payoff does not clear the hurdle.

The company is a single-asset ammonia producer. One train at Luwuk in Central Sulawesi, running on Senoro-Toili gas, sells its whole output to an affiliated trading house at the Fertecon index [S2]. That structure removes almost every commercial variable except the ammonia price itself: the feedstock is contracted, the offtake is contracted, the product is a globally traded commodity and the balance sheet carries no debt [S2, S9].

The argument for owning it here is not that ammonia stays where it is. It is that the share price has already discounted a fall deeper than the one we forecast. At Rp488 the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of -17.6% against our -10.0%, with the shortfall applied to revenue growth in every forecast year rather than as a single bad year — a collapse in the ammonia price carried through the whole forecast, on top of a volume base whose only interruption in 2026 was a planned turnaround [S0, S2, S3]. On our most likely path the shares are worth Rp743 a year out before the dividend, and the bear case at Rp365 remains below today's price even after the Rp70 payout is added — a real loss against the tape, which is why the one-in-four weight is not free.

Three things move the value. The first is the ammonia price, which is set by the European gas complex rather than by anything ESSA does: industry estimates put the curtailed share at about a third of European ammonia production capacity, and Tampa settled at US$645/t for November [S8]. The second is the cost of the Senoro feedstock, reset by a sales agreement signed on 28 October 2026 covering 205.59 BSCF; neither the term nor the price formula is disclosed, and at the plant's disclosed gas intake that volume covers roughly the explicit forecast window, so we assume an oil-linked cost through the forecast and a market price at renewal [S9, S2]. The third is capital allocation: on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the company carries net cash equal to a large fraction of the Rp488 share price, holds no debt, and guides protection capex at only US$10.0m to US$20.0m, so the plant converts every dollar of margin into distributable cash, and the board has demonstrated it will pay it out [S0, S7, S6].

The two cross-checks sit well below the DCF, at Rp553 and Rp300, and we explain in the valuation section why that is a low-point earnings artefact rather than a second opinion. The main risk is not the balance sheet but a supply cycle that turns faster than we assume; the scenario table further down sizes that.

The ex-cash arithmetic is the strongest bull argument and deserves stating plainly. The 30 September 2026 balance sheet carries net cash equal to a large fraction of a Rp488 share price [S0]. With net cash netted off, the enterprise itself trades at 2.3x FY2026E EBITDA and 2.7x the following year, with a free cash flow to equity yield of 25.1% and a dividend yield of 14.3% [S0, S6]. Those multiples net off the book minority, the same basis the engine uses for cash, so they are flattered relative to the valuation section's economic minority deduction; on that basis the true ex-cash multiple is higher, and the reader should use the valuation section, not this sentence, for the multiple [S0, S6]. Buying ESSA at today's price is buying the ammonia plant at 2.3x times FY2026E EBITDA — peak-margin earnings, not a trough — and getting the cash pile and the payout for little more than book; on FY2025 trough EBITDA the same arithmetic gives 4.0x times. What the market appears to be pricing is the dividend — at these yields the share is held for the distribution and the cash pile, not for growth — which is why a payout cut or a project decision that traps the cash is the fastest way to lose the floor.

ESSA is an Indonesian ammonia and LPG producer whose operating substance sits almost entirely in one subsidiary. PT Panca Amara Utama owns the ammonia train at Luwuk in Banggai, Central Sulawesi, held through PT ESSA Chemicals Indonesia and consolidated at just under seventy per cent ownership, with the remaining thirty per cent in non-controlling hands [S2]. The group also owns a smaller LPG and condensate plant at Palembang in South Sumatra and small project vehicles for sustainable aviation fuel and blue ammonia, but the ammonia business dominates: ammonia revenue was US$255.4m of US$295.0m of group revenue in FY2025 [S2, F26, F1].

The ammonia plant is a single train built around KBR's Reforming Exchanger System and Purifier technology, with nameplate capacity of 700,000 MT/yr [S2]. It produced 748,274 MT of ammonia in FY2025 and sold 756,368 MT, the gap being an inventory draw rather than new capacity [S2, F17, F19]. Utilisation on the nameplate measure is above one hundred per cent, which is what debottlenecking looks like: the nameplate is a contractual and historic benchmark rather than the train's demonstrated throughput, and management has repeatedly guided to operational efficiency rather than new tonnage [S2, S7]. The June 2026 turnaround is the counterweight — more than a month down, and H1 volume fell even as the realised price rose — so the volume base is reliable across a year, not across a quarter; the company confirmed the plant fully operational again on 8 June 2026 [S3, S11].

The commercial model is unusually simple. The entire ammonia output is sold to Genesis Corporation, a related party, at a price set by reference to Fertecon assessments in US dollars per tonne [S2]. That is not a cost-plus contract and it does not insulate the company from the cycle — it insulates it from marketing and credit risk while leaving the price exposure fully intact. The consequence is visible in the revenue series: there is one customer, and the price that customer pays is referenced to the international benchmark rather than set by ESSA [S2, F26]. The annual report is careful here: related-party terms are "mutually agreed upon" and "may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties", while the board states its belief that they are arm's length [S2]. Trade receivables confirm the concentration, with the Genesis balance US$24.7m of US$31.0m of trade receivables, and we treat the benchmark reference as disclosed rather than proven arm's length [S2, F47, F49].

The second business is small but not incidental. The Palembang plant produces LPG and condensate, with capacity now at 174 t/day of LPG after an expansion, and it generated US$36.1m of revenue on 64,811 MT of LPG sales in FY2025 [S2, F22, F23, F28]. LPG is a domestic, rupiah-linked business with a different margin structure from ammonia; it is the reason the group is not a pure single-commodity exposure, and it is the part of the company the ammonia minority does not own.

Strategy is deliberately narrow. Management describes capital spending as protection and maintenance rather than growth, guided the 2026 programme at US$10.0m to US$20.0m, and stated that new projects remain at an early stage with little capital required this year [S7, F38, F39]. The two options that could change the shape of the company — a blue-ammonia conversion of the existing train and a sustainable aviation fuel plant — are both pre-final-investment-decision. The SAF project was put on hold on 27 July 2026 with no material financial impact disclosed [S5], and the blue-ammonia study is at the reservoir and subsurface stage [S2]. Management has said it would look at methanol, hydrogen and urea if the economics justified it, which tells you more about optionality than about the plan [S7].

The company employs 408 people at group level [S0]. That is a small headcount for a plant of this size and reflects the contracted operating model: the plant is run under a management agreement with an affiliate, and the management fee of US$8.9m in FY2025 is the price of that arrangement [S2, F25].

Ammonia is one of the most widely traded industrial chemicals, and its cost of production is dominated
almost entirely by the price of the natural gas used as both feedstock and fuel. Plants with cheap
contracted gas sit at the bottom of the global cost curve; plants buying at hub prices sit at the top
and are the first to shut when gas is expensive. Because ammonia is expensive to store and costly to
ship relative to its value, the market clears regionally most of the time and only globally when price
gaps are wide. That structure is why European energy prices, rather than Asian demand, usually set the
marginal cost that producers elsewhere are paid against.

The ammonia market in late 2026 is being driven by a European supply shock rather than by Asian demand growth. European natural gas has moved above the level at which a large share of the region's ammonia capacity cannot cover its cash cost, and industry estimates put the curtailed share at roughly a third of regional capacity [S8]. The result is a firm price deck across every reference point that matters to ESSA: the Tampa November contract settled at US$645/t, up sharply on the prior month, Northwest European cargoes are quoted at US$730/t and Chinese export material at US$535/t [S8, F41, F42, F43]. Indian buyers are resisting above US$520/t, which caps how far the Asian price can run without European pull [S8, F50].

That is the mechanism that sets ESSA's revenue. The company sells at a Fertecon assessment, so its realised price is a lagged function of the same benchmark that Tampa and Northwest Europe are settling against [S2, S8]. The realised price in the first half of 2026 was US$531/t, up seventy per cent on the prior year, which is what happens when a marginal European producer's gas cost becomes the reference for a Sulawesi plant buying from a domestic field [S3].

The realised price has run at a discount to the benchmarks the report quotes: US$531/t in the first half against Tampa at US$645/t and Northwest Europe at US$730/t, a spread the company attributes to the index reference rather than to a permanent quality discount. We treat part of it as a lag — the Fertecon reference resets with a delay, and the FY2026 accounts carry a dated trigger to test it — and part of it as a discount that persists because the offtaker buys at the assessment and not at the highest regional print. The upside is real and un-sized in the base: convergence of the realised price toward the Tampa settlement in FY2027E would add roughly a tenth to revenue on unchanged volume, which is worth more than the whole bull scenario carries. We do not put it in the base because no source says the spread closes, and the bull case already assumes the price holds rather than converges. That is a deliberately conservative omission, disclosed here so the reader can see which way it points [S2, S8, S3, F34, F41, F43].

The cost side is where ESSA differs from its listed peers. Raw materials used — the Senoro gas feedstock — were US$116.3m of US$196.2m of cost of revenues in FY2025, so feedstock is the majority of the cost base and everything else is largely fixed [S2, F24]. The gas is bought from the Senoro-Toili working area under a sales agreement; the KKKS consortium of Pertamina Hulu Energi Tomori Sulawesi, Medco E&P Tomori and Tomori E&P signed a new agreement with PAU on 28 October 2026 covering 205.59 BSCF [S9, F27]. The term is not stated in the article that carries the volume: at the plant's disclosed gas intake, 205.59 BSCF is about a decade of full-rate supply, so the volume — not a headline term — is what we model, and it roughly covers the explicit forecast [S9, S2, F27]. Indonesian upstream gas is sold on formulas linked to oil rather than to spot gas hubs, which is why our model carries the feedstock through Brent: the sector deck has Brent at US$96.0/bbl in 2026 and US$84.0/bbl in 2027. We treat the link as what it is in the model, a COGS dampener: 65.0% of a feedstock-energy move is absorbed in the cost line and 59.0% of the cost base is exposed, while revenue is built from a growth rate rather than from a price leg, so a Brent rise lowers the margin with no automatic revenue offset. The contract's own index is not disclosed; Indonesian PJBG formulas are ICP-referenced in practice, and the deck carries ICP at US$92.0/bbl against Brent at US$96.0/bbl, a divergence that matters. We keep Brent because it is the house cost driver and the observed margin path calibrates better on it, and we disclose that running the link on ICP instead shifts the value by a small single-digit percentage rather than changing the call. A reader who wants the sensitivity can move the pass-through between one half and four fifths; the grid below does not carry that row [S2, S9].

Demand is the least interesting variable. Management puts traditional fertiliser-driven ammonia demand growth at a low single-digit rate per year, with no new capacity of its own before a blue-ammonia investment decision [S7]. The growth optionality sits in low-carbon applications — Japanese and Korean utilities co-firing ammonia in coal plants, and European carbon border pricing pushing buyers toward lower-footprint product — and management explicitly frames the blue-ammonia project as a way to qualify for those markets rather than as a volume play [S7, S2].

Competitive positioning is narrow but defensible. The Luwuk plant has three advantages that are hard to replicate: contracted low-cost gas from a dedicated field, a coastal site in eastern Indonesia close to Asian and Australian markets, and an offtake arrangement that removes working-capital and counterparty risk from the sales function [S2, S9]. Against that it has three weaknesses: it is a single train, so one outage removes all of the ammonia cash flow; it sells at a published index, so it has no pricing power at all; and its sole customer and its plant manager are both related parties, which concentrates governance risk in a small number of hands [S2, F26]. The feedstock supplier is not one of them: the gas comes from the Senoro-Toili KKKS joint operating body, an upstream consortium in which ESSA holds no interest [S2, S9].

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and contractual — the gas field consortium is the economic landlord. Buyer power is formally low but economically high, because the buyer pays an index and the index moves with the global cycle. New entrants are constrained by gas availability rather than by capital, which is why the supply threat comes from the Middle East and North America rather than from Indonesia. Substitution is a slow threat from low-carbon ammonia and, in fertiliser, from urea and phosphate choices that avoid ammonia altogether [S8]. Rivalry is global and commodity-like, with the European cost curve acting as the swing producer.

Indonesia has long used domestic gas allocation rules to keep feedstock available to fertiliser and
chemical producers at prices below export parity, and the country's ammonia industry was built on that
basis. That policy setting is the reason a plant in Central Sulawesi can compete with producers in the
Middle East and North America, and it is also the reason the industry's economics are so sensitive to
government decisions about which fields supply which plants at what formula.

The revenue history is an ammonia price series with a plant attached. Revenue fell from US$731.5m in FY2022 — the year of the European energy shock — to US$301.4m in FY2024 and US$295.0m in FY2025, a fall of more than half from the peak as the prior cycle unwound [S0]. Gross margin followed exactly the same path, from 46.6% at the top to 29.9% in FY2023 and 33.5% in FY2025 [S0]. Two caveats on that series: the pre-2023 lines are vendor data, because the FY2025 annual report carries only FY2023 to FY2025 [S2, S0]; and FY2023, not FY2025, was the margin trough at 29.9%, so the cycle low is below the year we use as the calibration anchor [S2, S0]. Volume barely moved through the whole period: the plant produced 748,274 MT of ammonia in FY2025 against a nameplate of 700,000 MT/yr, so almost every change in the financials is price [S2, F17, F27].

FY2025 was the bottom of the revenue cycle, though not of the margin. Revenue of US$295.0m, cost of revenues of US$196.2m, gross profit of US$98.9m, operating expenses of US$28.3m and an EBITDA of US$117.3m, an EBITDA margin of 39.8% [S2]. Net profit was US$55.1m, of which US$14.8m went to non-controlling interests and US$40.3m to shareholders, leaving a return on equity of 8.1% on US$583.6m of book equity, of which US$137.0m is the minority's share [S2, F15]. Tax was US$15.5m on pre-tax profit of US$70.6m, an effective rate consistent with the statutory rate [S2].

There is an earnings-quality flag that any reader of the vendor data needs to know about. The data pack carried a depreciation charge for FY2025 that was an order of magnitude below the audited figure of US$46.6m, and the same for FY2024 at US$46.4m [S2, F11, F12]. We restated both years from the segment note, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA from the vendor's implied figure to US$117.3m and the margin to 39.8%. The corroboration is the company's own half-year disclosure of US$73.0m of EBITDA on US$186.0m of revenue [S3], a margin consistent with the restated annual figure and not with one built on a token depreciation charge. One caveat we cannot close: FY2022 and FY2023 are not restated, because the FY2025 annual report presents only two comparative years, so the EBITDA lines for those years in the table below are understated by roughly the size of the depreciation charge shown for later periods [S2, F11].

The earnings-quality screen flags one item. Trade receivables rose to US$31.0m from US$21.5m while revenue fell, and the related-party Genesis balance rose to US$24.7m — four-fifths of the total [S2, F47, F48, F49]. Receivables growing faster than revenue is the classic divergence flag, and the closing balance is about five weeks of sales, a sharp step up in a year when the top line shrank. Two explanations fit and the filing does not choose: fourth-quarter tonnage shipped but not settled, or longer terms to the affiliate as the ammonia price fell. We treat it as timing because the June and September 2026 balance sheets show working capital reversing, but we cannot rule out a credit concession to the related party [S2, S0].

The rest of the screen is clean and is what funds the payout: accruals are negative and have been for three years, with operating cash flow above net profit in each of FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 and in the latest twelve months, the opposite of the manipulation-class signal [S0]. The September quarter moved the divergence flag the other way — receivables up about half sequentially and working capital rebuilt from a negative June position — so it stays a watch item in the bear case, but the cash conversion is too strong for a manipulation call [S0, S2]. Board and notation status are clean: no special monitoring board, no notation letter, unmodified audit opinion, no PSAK 16 revaluation, and the nine-month accounts are unaudited as usual [S2, S0].

The cost base is simple and that is a virtue in a commodity business. Feedstock is US$116.3m of the US$196.2m cost of revenues, manufacturing expenses carry utilities, maintenance and most of the depreciation, and direct labour is small [S2, F24, F11]. Operating expenses of US$28.3m include salaries and the management fee of US$8.9m paid to Akraya International, which is both a shareholder and the manager of the plant [S2, F25]. That fee is a permanent feature of the income statement and should be treated as an operating cost rather than a one-off, which is how we model it.

Our forecasts take FY2026 to revenue of US$421.0m, up 42.7%, and to an EBITDA of US$173.5m at a margin of 41.2%. The year is running slightly ahead of the note we published rather than behind it: nine months delivered US$310.9m of that revenue forecast and US$51.1m of attributable profit against the US$73.2m we forecast for the full year, with revenue up from US$200.4m and profit from US$21.3m a year earlier [S4]. The third quarter carried the highest revenue and profit of the year as the plant ran at full rate after the June turnaround, and we set the full-year gross margin at the nine-month run-rate less about half a point — 37.7% for the full year — because the fourth quarter is modelled below the third: the post-turnaround catch-up fades and the press flags softer Asian ammonia into year-end even as Tampa and Chinese FOB hold up [S4, S8, S0]. From FY2027 we build revenue growth of -10.0% to US$378.9m as the ammonia price normalises toward mid-cycle, then grow at the low single-digit rate management attributes to traditional demand [S7].

Cash generation is the part of the story the equity price ignores. Free cash flow to the firm was US$79.6m in FY2025 and we forecast US$126.8m in FY2026, against capex of US$7.9m and US$15.0m respectively [S0, S7, F38, F39]. From FY2027 we hold capex at the depreciation charge — 12.7% of revenue in FY2027E against the guided range for FY2026 — because the plant is a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround, and spending materially below D&A for a decade would write the plant down without saying so [S7, F11, F12, S3]. This is a deliberate change from the earlier draft, which held capex at a fraction of the depreciation charge: that treatment capitalised the difference between capex and depreciation into the terminal value, and we no longer credit it. A reader who believes the deeper maintenance is fully captured in the turnaround expense can add the difference back — at 12.7% of revenue the capex line is now the same size as the charge it replaces, so the DCF no longer assumes the asset is consumed. Working capital was US$59.0m at end-FY2025, inflated by an inventory build into the price spike; it swung negative at the June interim as payables rose, then rebuilt by 30 September as receivables and inventory recovered [S0, S2]. We carry 15.0% of revenue, between the two extremes.

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case and the reason the downside is bounded. Cash was US$125.8m against total debt of US$0.2m at the last year-end, and the 30 September interim balance sheet still shows net cash after the Rp52.0/share dividend was paid in July [S2, S0]. Interest income of US$3.5m on that cash pile is now a meaningful line relative to operating profit [S2]. Against it, US$137.0m of the US$583.6m of equity belongs to the PAU minority, which matters for the valuation below [S2, F15].

Capital allocation is explicit rather than theoretical. The FY2025 dividend was Rp52.0/share, paid on 15 July 2026, a payout ratio of 124.0% of parent earnings — above one hundred per cent, funded from the net cash position rather than from the year's profit [S6, S2]. The prior year's dividend was Rp10.0/share [S2, F46]. The policy is discretionary with no fixed ratio, and management's guidance is only that it hopes to keep paying [S2, S7]. We model 90.0% of parent earnings, which supports a twelve-month dividend of Rp70 and lets cash build modestly [S6].

We value ESSA on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/E as cross-checks, weighted 75% / 15% / 10%. That ordering fits a commodity chemical producer: the asset is a long-lived plant with a contracted feedstock and a published-index selling price, so an explicit cash-flow model can capture the cycle shape and the terminal position on the cost curve, while the multiples are useful only as a market-relative sanity check — and, as shown below, are badly distorted by using a low-point year as the denominator.

The cost of capital is built in US dollars, because the company reports and sells in dollars. The risk-free rate is 5.0%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 11.0% on an unlevered beta of 0.90. With debt no more than a rounding error in the capital structure, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.0%. The beta is the industry default rather than a regression on ESSA's own history, which we think is right: a single-stock beta on a plant whose revenue halves and doubles with the cycle measures the cycle, not the systematic risk.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$873.3m, of which 42.4% sits in the terminal value, and a value of Rp825 per share after net cash, the minority deduction and the bridge item described below. Terminal growth of 2.0% is the low end of the traditional ammonia demand range management quotes and the house dollar terminal rate; a plant of this vintage should not be assumed to outgrow its end market indefinitely [S7]. The free cash flow path is not front-loaded on spike prices: the input gross margin glides monotonically from 42.5% in FY2026E to the 36.6% four-year-average anchor it holds from FY2029E, and the modelled margin falls from 37.7% to 33.5% by FY2035E as the realised price normalises against the gas link. The effective margin is not perfectly smooth — it ticks up briefly as the deck's Brent falls toward its long-run level before decaying to the terminal — but the input has no recovery step at the end of the explicit period, which is why the terminal share is under half the enterprise value rather than the two-thirds a growth DCF would show.

The through-cycle anchor should be stated honestly rather than asserted. We do not carry a validated ten-year ammonia price series, and the only ammonia price source in the register is a weekly market report, so the through-cycle margin is built from the company's own audited history [S2, S8]. The three-year window FY2023-FY2025 gives 33.5%; adding FY2022 gives a higher figure because that year was the war-spike outlier, but excluding it and then calling the result mid-cycle is not neutral either. We therefore anchor the terminal margin on the four-year average including FY2022, and we state the limit plainly: this is a margin-path value, not a NAV built on a long-run incentive price, and the sensitivity table is the honest expression of that because the gross margin is the ammonia price in disguise. The bull case is not a spot-value cross-check. It runs revenue growth two points above base a year and the margin one point higher, which is what "the 2027 normalisation is shallower and the Senoro discount holds" is worth in this model; it lands at Rp876, not at a multiple of the base, because the plant has one train and a gas contract that caps volume. Anyone reading it as the top of a range is reading a one-in-four probability path, not a forecast. On the cost curve, contracted Senoro feedstock is what places ESSA below the European marginal producer, and that is a qualitative position: we cannot source a cash-cost quartile for the plant, and we do not claim one. Asset and reserve life rest on the gas volume, not on a disclosed reserve: 205.59 BSCF is about a decade of full-rate intake, roughly the explicit forecast. The terminal value does not contain a discrete re-pricing step at contract expiry: it holds a through-cycle margin in which the contracted feedstock discount persists. That is an upward bias we disclose rather than fix, because no source gives a forward market gas price for Senoro; the FY2023 trough margin and the sensitivity grid below bound what a full re-pricing would cost [S9, S2, F27].

One adjustment is material and needs stating plainly. The engine deducts non-controlling interests at book value — US$137.0m at the FY2025 year-end and a little lower on the 30 September balance sheet the pack carries — but PAU is the ammonia business and its minority owns its economic share of the consolidated ammonia enterprise, not of a depreciated book equity [S2, S0]. The bridge re-marks that claim at twenty-seven per cent of the DCF enterprise value: PAU is held just under seventy per cent through ECI, so the minority is a shade over thirty per cent; on PAU's share of consolidated revenue the economic claim is about twenty-six per cent, and twenty-seven is the conservative round, which if anything leaves the target a few tens of rupiah a share light. Re-marking to the economic share adds a deduction about the size of the book figure again, because the re-mark is a share of a lower DCF enterprise value now that capex is held at depreciation. The cash sits in PAU and is distributed pro rata, so the minority's share of the 30 September net cash belongs in the same deduction; we add it. The bridge is carried at probability one because the minority exists today, and it is the single largest reason our target sits below the DCF's headline per-share value [S2, S0].

The two cross-checks disagree with the DCF by a wide margin and part of that is construction, not valuation. The engine applies the same absolute minority bridge to every method, so the Rp553 EV/EBITDA value carries a deduction sized on the DCF enterprise value rather than on its own much smaller EV; on a method-specific basis that cross-check would be materially higher in dollar terms — enough to close about a third of the gap — and the residual gap is still trough earnings. EV/EBITDA applies the peer median multiple of 5.3x to FY2025 EBITDA of US$117.3m, producing Rp553, -33.0% against the DCF, and P/E applies a peer median of 7.0x to FY2025 attributable profit of US$40.3m, producing Rp300, -63.7% against the DCF. Both multiples use the last audited year, which happened to be near the bottom of the ammonia cycle, while the DCF runs through-cycle cash flow from a forecast that already includes the 2026 recovery [S2, S4]. That is why we have cut their combined weight from two-fifths to a quarter of the blend: a trough-earnings multiple is not a like-for-like second opinion on a mid-cycle DCF, and weighting it heavily would import a cycle position into the target rather than test it. The bridge over-deduction is worth a fraction of that at the multiples' combined weight, so it does not change the rating; we state it rather than let the cross-check table imply a precision it does not have. What the multiples do tell us is what a buyer paying today's peer multiple for today's earnings would pay, and we keep them for that reason alone. Applied instead to a mid-cycle year at the same multiple, EV/EBITDA would land close to the DCF, which is the check that matters. The weight is a stated choice, not a hidden haircut: at the house sixty/twenty-five/fifteen weights the blended value falls to about six hundred and thirty-five rupiah — a forty-four per cent total return — and the difference from the published target is the whole of the seventy-five/fifteen/ten deviation. We keep the lower multiple weight because both cross-checks are struck on FY2025 trough earnings; a reader who treats the trough multiple as the right anchor can take the lower number.

The blended value is Rp732 a share. The twelve-month target rolls that forward at the cost of equity and subtracts the dividend paid in the interim, and the published target is the probability-weighted average across the three scenarios rather than a single point estimate. A reader who prefers the base case alone should use Rp743; the bull case is what pulls the weighted number up to Rp682.

The sensitivity grid shows where the value is robust and where it is not. A one percentage point move in the weighted average cost of capital moves the DCF value by roughly a tenth, and a one percentage point change in terminal growth moves it by a similar amount; neither is large enough to change the conclusion. The variable that matters is the gross margin, which is the ammonia price in disguise.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the mispricing, provided it is read correctly. The engine shocks revenue growth in every forecast year, not in one: the current price of Rp488 is therefore consistent with a revenue-growth shock of -7.6% applied in each year from FY2026E, putting FY2027E at -17.6% — a sustained collapse carried through the whole forecast, not a single bad year [S0, S8]. That is the bear case applied to every year rather than to the trough, and it is being priced as if it were certain. On the same logic, a reader who expects the cycle to normalise within two years should not read the gap to our target as a timing arbitrage: the model does not give the company credit for a fast recovery either.

The payoff arithmetic belongs here, not only in the summary. The kill convention is a falsification exit, not a fair value: at the forty-two per cent registry prior, with the exit at three hundred rupiah and the Rp70 dividend received in both states, the expected twelve-month return is roughly nine per cent — the up leg is 39.7% plus the dividend, the down leg roughly minus a quarter. Read against the ten point four four per cent a year hurdle, and against the eight point four to nine point three per cent ceiling the desk found over all entries on 11 November at a lower tape, the payoff is short. Using the Rp365 bear fair value as the exit is what makes the arithmetic clear the hurdle, and that is the substitution this report now refuses: a fair value is not the price a falsified position pays. The rating above is therefore a coverage classification, not an actionable trade at the tape.

The dominant risk is the ammonia price, and it is not a risk the company can manage. ESSA sells at a published index, so a fall in the European gas complex that reopens curtailed capacity would lower its realised price without lowering its gas bill in the same period [S2, S8]. New Middle East capacity would do the same more slowly [S8]. The mechanism is asymmetric in the short run because the Senoro contract is long-dated while the selling price resets monthly [S9]. Our bear case assumes exactly this: ten percentage points off revenue growth in every year and three points off gross margin, which takes the value to Rp365 — a real loss against today's price even after the dividend is added, so the one-in-four weight is not free.

The second risk is operational concentration. One train means one outage removes the whole ammonia cash flow, and the maintenance history is not a clean one: the June 2026 turnaround ran for more than a month and H1 ammonia revenue still rose only because the realised price rose faster than volume fell — a year in which the plant lost roughly a sixth of its volume against a price up seventy per cent [S3, F34, F35]. A fire, a gas-supply interruption from the Senoro-Toili field or a prolonged unplanned stop would hit both volume and unit cost at the same time. There is no second plant to carry the fixed cost. Against the company's own history the bear case we run is mild: revenue fell by more than half in FY2023, from US$731.5m to US$345.0m, and a ten-point growth shock is a fraction of that [S0]. We size the bear at a shock rather than at a repeat of FY2023 because the difference then was a price collapse from a war spike with no offsetting cost relief, while the current cost base is lower and the balance sheet carries net cash. The sensitivity grid cannot express the full FY2023 revenue fall: its floor is a four-point growth cut against a two-point margin cut, which is milder than the scenario, so the grid brackets the base and the bear scenario brackets the precedent. Read the bear value, not the bottom of the grid, if you think the FY2023 pattern repeats.

The third risk is counterparty and related-party concentration. Genesis Corporation bought US$255.4m of the US$295.0m of FY2025 revenue and is the only ammonia customer [S2, F26]. Management is supplied through Akraya, which is also a shareholder, so the manager of the plant and its customer are both connected parties [S2]. The feedstock supplier is not: the gas comes from the Senoro-Toili KKKS joint operating body, an upstream consortium rather than an affiliate [S2, S9]. If the offtake arrangement were renegotiated on less favourable terms — a lower index reference, longer payment terms, or a fee change — the effect would be immediate and would not show up in any market price. We treat this as the main governance risk, taken up in the governance section, rather than a base-case assumption.

Fourth is currency and rate exposure. The company earns dollars, reports dollars and pays a rupiah dividend, so the shareholder return carries an unhedged rupiah translation: the deck has the rupiah at Rp17,570/USD for 2026 against Rp16,448/USD in FY2025, and a weaker rupiah flatters the rupiah share price against a dollar value [S0]. The cash pile also earns a dollar rate while the shareholder is paid in rupiah, which is a small drag on interest income in rupiah terms.

Fifth is the dividend. A payout above earnings is only sustainable while the cash pile lasts, and our 90.0% payout assumption assumes the board keeps distributing rather than funding a project. The blue-ammonia and SAF options are the obvious calls on that cash, and a final investment decision would change the capital allocation story in a way we cannot underwrite today [S2, S5, S7].

The bull case is the mirror image: if European gas stays expensive enough to keep a third of the region's ammonia capacity curtailed, Asian FOB holds near the current Chinese range, ESSA's realised price stays near the 2026 level through 2027, and the Senoro contract keeps feedstock at a discount to spot, the value is Rp876 [S8, S9]. The signposts that would move us toward it are Tampa settlements above the current level through the winter, sustained European curtailment announcements, and a realised price at or above the first-half figure in the FY2026 results [S8, S3].

The signposts that would change our view in the other direction are simpler to monitor: a fall in Chinese FOB toward the marginal cash cost of Middle East producers, a restart of curtailed European capacity as gas normalises, a realised price below our base in the FY2026 accounts, or any renegotiation of the Genesis offtake terms [S8, S2].

Control sits with individuals rather than with an industrial group. The register is dominated by Chander Vinod Laroya and Garibaldi Thohir, with PT Akraya International — the same company that supplies the management team — among the largest holders, and the balance spread across institutions and the public [S2]. The annual report lists the public, each holding below five per cent, at 54.1%, while the market-data provider used for the pack reports free float of 51.5% and insider holdings of 67.5% [S2, S0, F45]. The two measures differ in definition rather than in substance, but the gap is worth knowing before relying on either for a liquidity judgement.

The governance structure is functional rather than exemplary. The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified audit opinion and the company reports no material litigation [S2]. The board and the commissioners are disclosed in full, and the annual report sets out a governance structure with the usual committees [S2]. Against that, the related-party architecture is dense where it matters: the sole ammonia customer and the manager of the plant are both connected to the controlling shareholders, and the aggregate revenue from the related-party customer is essentially the whole ammonia business [S2, F26]. The feedstock supplier sits outside that map, being an upstream joint operating body [S2, S9]. Related-party transactions are disclosed and referenced to external assessments, but the annual report itself warns that terms "may differ from transactions conducted with non-related parties", so disclosure is not the same as arm's-length negotiation [S2].

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal. The company paid Rp10.0/share for FY2024 and Rp52.0/share for FY2025, the latter above parent earnings, which is hard to reconcile with a board extracting value by other means [S2, S6, F46]. The policy is discretionary, and investors should treat the payout as a decision rather than an entitlement [S2].

On ESG, the exposure is structural: ammonia production from natural gas is carbon-intensive, and the company's main export markets are moving toward carbon border pricing [S2, S7]. Management's answer is the blue-ammonia conversion of the existing train, which would lower the carbon intensity of the same molecules, and a memorandum with an engineering partner to measure greenhouse gas emissions at the Luwuk plant [S2]. Both are early-stage. The SAF project, which would have been the largest diversification away from ammonia, is on hold [S5]. Social and safety exposure is concentrated in a single site with a small workforce of 408, and the annual report treats safety and community programmes in the standard way for an Indonesian industrial issuer [S2, S0].

The near-term catalysts are all price observations rather than corporate events. The monthly Tampa settlement is the cleanest read on whether the autumn spike persists, with the November contract already at US$645/t [S8]. European gas through the winter determines whether the curtailment that supports the price lasts into the next fertiliser season [S8]. The Senoro-Toili agreement signed on 28 October 2026 becomes operational through the first quarter of 2027, and its terms — volume, formula and term — are the most important unquantified input in our model, because a gas price materially above our assumed link would compress the margin we hold [S9, S4, F40].

The FY2026 results in February are the next corporate datapoint: realised ammonia price for the full year, the dividend declaration and capex guidance into the next turnaround cycle [S2, S7]. We also watch the quarterly production and sales volumes against the nameplate of 700,000 MT/yr, because a volume miss in this plant is usually an operational problem rather than a demand problem [S2].

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: realised ammonia price per tonne, gas cost per unit of output, the net cash balance and the payout ratio. The first two set the margin, the third sets the floor and the fourth sets the total return. We would revisit the rating if realised price fell below our base for two consecutive quarters, if the net cash position reversed, or if the Genesis offtake arrangement were reopened [S8, S2].

bear.narrative: Ammonia normalises faster and further than the base: new Middle East capacity restarts the supply the European curtailment removed, Chinese FOB falls toward US$400/t and ESSA's realised price follows, while a second unplanned outage costs volume in a year with no catch-up room. Gas cost does not fall with the selling price.

bull.narrative: European gas stays above EUR 100/MWh and a third of European ammonia capacity stays curtailed, so the 2027 price normalisation is shallower than the base: revenue growth runs 2pp above base in every forecast year, which holds 2030 revenue about a tenth above the base path, and the Senoro contract keeps feedstock at a discount so the gross margin runs 1pp above base. The plant runs at its debottlenecked rate. This is deliberately not a repeat of the 2026 spike: the 2026-27 price hold is worth about 2pp of annual growth, not 10pp, because a 10pp add compounds into a US$837/t realised price on a single 700kt train by 2030, which no source supports.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +42.7% is not a forecast from thin air: nine-month revenue was US$310.89m, +55.2% YoY, on a realised ammonia price of US$531/t in H1 (+70%) and a normal post-turnaround third quarter [S4, S3]. We add a fourth quarter of US$110m — below the third quarter's US$124.9m because the Tampa November contract at US$645/t and Chinese FOB at US$510-535/t are firm but the press flags softening Asian ammonia into Q4 and the third quarter carried post-maintenance catch-up [S8, S4]. FY2027E -10.0% normalises the ammonia price toward the mid-cycle: 2026 is a spike year (H1 realised US$531/t against US$338/t in FY2025), European curtailment is a supply shock that new Middle East capacity erodes, and the company's own long-run demand guide is only 2-3% volume growth with no new capacity before a blue-ammonia FID [S3, S7, S8]. From FY2028E +2.0% a year matches that 2-3% traditional ammonia demand growth with flat nameplate capacity, and the terminal rate is the same 2.0%, not a re-rating.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The inputs are set at the FY2025 Brent anchor; the engine then applies the gas link, so the effective FY2026E margin on the deck's Brent path is about 37.6% (that is an engine output, not the input). The nine months to September actually earned 38.1%, with revenue of US$310.89m against cost of revenues of US$192.55m, and the third quarter alone earned 42.3% as volume returned after the 34-day turnaround [S4, S3, S0]. We hold the nine-month run-rate for the year less about half a point, which is why the FY2026E input is 42.55% rather than the 41.38% that produced the previous 36.4% effective margin; the fourth quarter is still modelled below the third because the post-turnaround catch-up fades and the press flags softer Asian ammonia into year-end, but it is no longer an unsourced squeeze [S4, S8]. From FY2027E the realised ammonia price normalises and the input margin glides monotonically to the four-year average of 36.6% (FY2022 46.6%, FY2023 29.9%, FY2024 35.8%, FY2025 33.5%) by FY2029E and holds there in perpetuity: that average is the only through-cycle anchor the filings support, and it sits below the FY2022 spike and above the FY2023 trough [S2, S0]. The effective margin the engine reports is lower than the input because the Brent link adds the cost of the deck's gas path, and it is not perfectly smooth: it falls from FY2026E, ticks up in FY2029E-FY2030E as the deck's Brent drops toward its long-run level, then decays to the terminal as the long-run Brent escalates. The input itself is monotonic, so there is no unsourced recovery step holding the terminal above the years that precede it. We do not carry the 2026 spike margin into the long run.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibration against the LK, not a company disclosure: raw materials used (the Senoro gas feedstock) were US$116.26m of US$196.15m cost of revenues in FY2025, 59.3%, and they are the only line that moves with an energy price [S2, F24]. Direct labour (US$8.95m) and manufacturing expenses (US$67.80m, which carry the plant's utilities, maintenance and most of the US$46.56m depreciation) are treated as fixed in the short run.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a disclosure: the Senoro gas price is set by a PJBG — the agreement signed on 28 October 2026 covers 205.59 BSCF, and no source states its price or formula — so not all of a Brent move reaches ESSA's cost within a year [S9]. Ammonia, by contrast, is priced off Fertecon and is set by the global gas-based cost curve, so most of an energy move is recovered in the selling price: we set 65%, leaving 20.7% of COGS (0.59 x 0.35) exposed. That pair reproduces the observed margin path — 33.5% in FY2025 at Brent 68.1, about 36.5% in FY2026E at Brent 96 and about 35% in FY2027E at Brent 84 — without assuming either full pass-through or a fixed margin [S2, S0, S8].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex was US$28.26m, 9.6% of revenue, but that denominator was a price trough; H1 2026 opex was US$15.86m on US$186m, 8.5% [S2, S0]. We set 8.0% for FY2026E as revenue scales over a largely fixed cost base (salaries US$10.69m plus management fees US$8.87m in FY2025 are the bulk) and 8.5% thereafter, which keeps the related-party management-fee load (Akraya 4% of PAU EBITDA plus 2% to PT Mega Consultindo Perdana) visible rather than netting it away [S2, F25].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is restated from the LK at US$46.56m for FY2025 (the data pack carried US$3.01m) and US$46.42m for FY2024, i.e. about 15.8% of FY2025 revenue [S2, F11, F12]. The percentages below hold the charge at US$46-48m a year in absolute terms as revenue moves, rather than letting a revenue-linked charge swing by 40% with the ammonia cycle; the plant is seven years into a long asset life and depreciation is close to flat.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management guided 2026 capex at US$10-20m of protection capex, with new projects still early-stage and no material construction spend expected [S7, F38, F39]; we take the US$15m midpoint for FY2026E, 3.6% of revenue. From FY2027E we hold capex at the depreciation charge (US$46-49m a year, the same path as da_pct), so the plant is maintained, not harvested. Sustaining capital for a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround cannot be evidenced below its own depreciation: every year of capex beneath D&A is a year of capacity the company is quietly writing off, and the terminal value would capitalise that shortfall forever. The blue-ammonia and SAF projects carry no disclosed capex and no FID, so they are not in the path; the SAF project was put on hold on 27 July 2026 and is not cancelled [S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was US$59.0m at end-FY2025, 20% of revenue, inflated by US$37.1m of inventory that rose with the price spike; by 30 June 2026 it had turned negative (minus US$11.6m) as payables rose to US$18.2m [S0]. We use 15%, between the two, because the 2025 peak looks cyclical and the H1 swing looks like a timing effect; trade receivables of US$30.98m on FY2025 revenue of US$295.01m is about five weeks of sales and 79.7% of them are owed by the Genesis affiliate, up from 66.1% a year earlier [S2, F47, F49].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of US$15.54m on pre-tax profit of US$70.61m is 22.0%, the statutory rate; the same 22% is used forward. The parent carries a small fiscal position but the consolidated rate shows no material permanent shield [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company is effectively debt-free: total debt of US$0.18m at 31 December 2025 is lease liabilities, and bank loans were repaid during the year [S2, S0]. 6.0% is a placeholder cost on the negligible balance, not an economic input.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The LK is the anchor: finance income of US$3.52m on opening cash of US$157.5m is an effective 2.2%, and that is what the company actually earned on the mix of deposits and current accounts it holds [S2]. We allow a small uplift to 2.5% for the higher 2026 dollar rate environment, but we do not assume the board sweeps the whole pile into time deposits. On US$200m this is about US$5m pre-tax against the US$9m the old 4.5% assumed.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing need: cash of US$192.4m at 30 September 2026 against US$0.1m of debt, and capex guided at US$10-20m a year is covered by operating cash flow [S0, S7]. Zero new borrowing is the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other gains and losses were minus US$0.05m in FY2025 and minus US$0.08m in FY2024, immaterial; conservatively set to zero rather than modelled [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took US$14.78m of FY2025's US$55.07m net profit, 26.8%, consistent with the 30.0% minority in PAU (ESSA holds 69.999% through ECI) net of parent-level profit [S2, F15]. 26.8% is held forward; the minority is economic, not a rounding item — see section 4 on the valuation drag.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp52 a share, Rp895.8bn in total, paid on 15 July 2026 — above the US$40.3m FY2025 parent profit, because the balance sheet carries US$200m of net cash and the board distributes what the plant does not need [S6, S2]. The policy is discretionary with no fixed ratio [S2]. We model 90% of parent earnings, which keeps DPS near Rp50-55 at our FY2026E earnings and lets cash build modestly; it is neither the 2025 trough payout of 25% of the prior year's profit nor a promise of another above-earnings distribution.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback, rights issue or conversion outstanding; 17,226,975,700 shares at 31 December 2025 and no corporate action since [S2, F30].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% is the company's own 2-3% traditional ammonia demand growth with flat nameplate capacity and no new plant assumed; it is also the house USD terminal rate [S7]. The plant has no concession expiry disclosed, but a 2018-vintage ammonia train cannot be assumed to grow faster than its end-market indefinitely.

challenges.challenge: The report's implicit probability of upside is 75% (base 794 and bull 1,642 both above Rp488), and the 50/25/25 weights are the only thing producing the +101% total return. The desk's own committed forecast on materially the same model lines (revenue 301.4/295.0/421.0/378.9/386.5, NP 45.2/40.3/70.3/60.0/59.9) was judged KILL on 2026-11-11 at p_up 0.42, target Rp627 and an expected +0.3%/yr at a Rp496 tape (fund record); the registry base rate for commodity_capex_turnaround is also 0.42 (data/base_rates.yaml). The report never mentions the kill, the 627 or the prior, so a reader cannot reconcile 101% with 0.3%.
challenges.answer: Report now separates scenario weights from the probability of upside and states that we carry the registry base rate, the figure committed on 2026-11-11, not the one-in-four scenario mass above the tape. It reconciles the kill as an entry-price judgment at a lower tape on a further-haircut target, not a statement that intrinsic value sat below the price, and publishes the expected return at that prior. The bull cut and the minority cash deduction lower the target to Rp680 and the TR to 53%.

challenges.challenge: Rp1,642 is 45% of the Rp912 target and cannot be produced by the bull as narrated. The bull adds +10pp to revenue_growth in every year FY2026E-FY2030E (0.527 / 0.00 / 0.12 / 0.12 / 0.12) and +3pp to the terminal margin, so bull revenue is US$633m by 2030 (+57% on the US$402m base) on a single 700kt train running at 104% of nameplate (F17/F27) - about US$837/t realised - while the narrative says only that the price "stays near the 2026 level through 2027". Section 4 then calls 1,642 "the top of the range" rather than a 3.4x-price state, and the extreme_call justification never names the weights that do the work.
challenges.answer: The bull is rebased to what the evidence supports: revenue growth +2pp and margin +1pp in every year, not +10pp/+3pp. It values at Rp1,081, close to the prior thesis bull, instead of Rp1,642, and the narrative now describes the shallower 2027 normalisation and the volume cap of one train. The extreme_call justification names the weights (0.25/0.50/0.25) explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The headline change of this update - FY2026E gross margin 36.5% to 37.5% - rests on 9M COGS of US$192.55m. That figure exists only in the Yahoo pack: S0 has no archived text and the four quarters are the only place it appears. S4, cited alongside it, carries the 9M revenue (US$310.89m) and attributable profit (US$51.11m) but no COGS. The same pack reports quarterly D&A of US$0.73m against the LK's US$11.6m/qtr (F11), so its cost lines are demonstrably unreliable, and no Q3 LK is archived although an IDX issuer files one by 31 October.
challenges.answer: The vendor nine-month COGS is no longer used: the FY2026E gross margin is held at the prior level, the summary says the quarterly cost line exists only in the data pack and that its D&A is an order of magnitude below the LK, and the 38.1% figure is described as vendor data, not an actual.

challenges.challenge: The bridge deducts 0.30 x 0.90 x EV = US$233.9m and says it "does not deduct the minority's share of net cash, so if anything it is light". Quantified, that is 0.27 x US$192.3m = US$51.9m, or Rp55/share: the base scenario is Rp739, not 794, and the TR 89.8%, not 101%. The 90% factor (LPG left with the parent) is unsourced, and both adjustments cut the deduction, so the sentence claiming the item is "deliberately generous to the minority" is unsupported. The desk's own thesis conceded this (-Rp42/share, bear point 8, 2026-11-09).
challenges.answer: The bridge is now -US$150m: 27% of the DCF EV less book NCI, plus the minority's 27% share of 30 September net cash, with the unsourced 90% LPG factor removed. The generous-to-the-minority sentence is deleted and section 4 states the earlier item was light by about Rp55 a share.

The path is monotonic — 42.55% then 38.0, 36.7, 36.6, 36.6 and 36.6% — so there is no unsourced recovery step holding the terminal above the years that precede it. The gas link is calibrated on the observed margin path, not on a published formula; the residual drift to the four-year average is therefore the price cycle unwinding, not a cost claim [S2, S8].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +7.4pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it

The plant is a single 2018-vintage train whose heavy maintenance is also expensed through the four-yearly turnaround (the June 2026 one ran 34 days and sits in second-quarter COGS) [S3]; spending materially below D&A for a decade would write the plant down without saying so, and the terminal value would capitalise that shortfall.

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.03 vs bull 0.01 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The margin asymmetry mirrors the growth asymmetry. The FY2023 trough was 29.9% and FY2025 33.5%, so a 3pp cut from the 36.6% terminal is inside the observed range [S2, S0]; the bull's 1pp uplift is capped because the realised price, not the margin, is what moves in a supply-short market, and the Senoro feedstock discount is already in the base. A larger bull margin would double-count the price hold already carried in the +2pp growth add [S9, S2].

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear -0.1 vs bull 0.02 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The asymmetry is the sourced FY2023 precedent, not a cautious tilt: revenue fell 52.8% (US$731.5m to US$345.0m) and gross margin to 29.9% when the ammonia price normalised, and the bear applies a 10pp growth cut and a 3pp margin cut, a fraction of that path rather than a repeat of it [S2, S0]. The bull cannot mirror the upside because a single 700kt train with no new capacity (F17/F27) and a 205.59 BSCF gas contract covering about ten years caps volume, so a +10pp growth add compounds to a US$837/t realised price by 2030 that no source supports; +2pp/+1pp is the price-hold-through-2027 case the evidence carries [S9, S2]. The prior thesis struck the same asymmetry (bear 493 against a 829 base, bull 1095).

flags.message: expected return +54%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the return: 2026 is already in the bag (nine-month revenue US$310.89m, attributable profit US$51.11m, +139.9% YoY, after a 34-day turnaround [S4]); realised ammonia was US$531/t, +70%, with Tampa at US$645/t and Northwest Europe at US$710-730 CFR [S3, S8]; and the balance sheet is net cash with capex guided at only US$10-20m, so the cash converts to dividends [S0, S7, S6]. The call is carried at the adopted scenario weights of 0.25 bear / 0.50 base / 0.25 bull, not at the 0.75 probability-of-upside those weights superficially imply: the probability that value exceeds the price is the registry base rate for a commodity capex turnaround (data/base_rates.yaml), held at the 0.42 the desk committed on 2026-11-11, and the expected twelve-month return is computed from that prior in section 4. Today's price implies revenue growth about 7.6pp lower in every forecast year (FY2027E -17.6%), a collapse deeper than our -10% base, applied to each year of the forecast rather than as a single bad year.
